title: The Noun, And The Ending That Means Two Things
label: ch:hi-sangya
canDo: I can make any A1 noun plural, read the oblique form a noun takes in front of a postposition, and put a demonstrative in front of a noun.

payoff.summary: Read the clause a practice paper prints in a personal account -- do bhaashaaen boltii hai -- and tell a plural -e apart from an oblique one by the postposition behind it.
payoff.note: Closes four points using ZERO new nouns: every example is a word the track already taught, so the chapter is pure morphology on known vocabulary. HI-A1-N-07 wanted plural morphology and its note names the item, do bhaashaaen boltii hai, which appears in both papers. HI-A1-N-08 wanted the oblique, which is the -aa to -e bend the track has already taught FOUR TIMES on other kinds of word -- possessives, adjectives, the habitual, the past copula -- so this is the same system arriving on its last kind rather than a new one. HI-A1-POST-06 wanted ko, and its note is exactly right that only the fused mujhe was present; the lesson takes aapko apart to show ko was inside it. HI-A1-DET-03's note is PARTLY STALE: it says the corpus never puts yah or vah in front of a noun, and HI-C69-verb-last prints yah kitaab hai while HI-C78-pehla-paath prints vah kitaab padhtaa hai -- but neither is an atom, so the point was genuinely uncovered and the precise complaint is that the shape is SHOWN and never TAUGHT. The chapter's load-bearing observation is that -e means two different things, plural and singular-oblique, and the postposition behind the noun is the only signal -- a reader who misses it miscounts every sentence that has one.
